title: Wankel_Text-Discussion_Chronicler-and-the-Modern-World_Linda, Kaljundi; Kļavinš, Kaspars
body:
1)    What is the text about? 

The work outlines the reception through the ages of the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, throughout written history of the Baltic Region following its translations and reinterpretations by contemporary historians who interpreted the work in various ways and through a variety of lenses depending on their agendas and temporal needs. Apparently Henry the Livonian held a position of prominence as a spectral companion alongside historians and authors as a result of his chronicles eliciting an obsessive need by generations of writers to alternately confirm or deny, uphold or debunk his body of work which described features of ancient Estonia and Latvia, and their relationship with the crusades, religion, and nobility.  


2)    What do you think are the main points of text? 

a) (Late 18th Century) Baltic Enlightenment laid the foundation for future (mainly nationalist) interpretations of Henry's works. 

b) During latter centuries, historians have alternated positive and negative reinterpretations of the Chronicle and of Henry's motivations. 

c) Different nationalities hold varying relationships to the Chronicles, and have used them in various ways to represent their own national identities. 


3)    Is there anything in these texts that stands out to you as similar or different to the history writing of your people/country/region/etc?

The fixation on a single text, and need for continuous reinterpretation reflects the attitudes surrounding the founding documents of the United States of America. The alternate attribution of heroism vs accusations of despotism toward the authors is reminiscent of the attitudes toward Henry through the centuries. 

 
4)    (Optional) Is there anything in Estonian history you are particularly interested in?

I am interested in the effect that previous colonization and repression have had on Estonian society and identity.

title: Wankel_Text-Discussion_From National Awakening to Independence_Kruusmaa_Kaljundi
body:
1)    What were the main arguments of (Baltic-)Germans in justifying or opposing serfdom? How do these fit into the wider context of pro-slavery thought (Kruusmaa)? 

According to Kruusmaa, Baltic-German elites often justified serfdom as beneficial to the populations on whom it was imposed. The prevailing thought at the time seemed to be that there was a hierarchy of value among "savages" and Estonian and Latvian peasants did not rank very high. Serfdom was framed not as exploitation but as a way of ensuring order, productivity, and even moral improvement. The prevailing narrative of the time depicted a harmonious existence of serfs, and excellent relations with their masters. Wider pro-slavery arguments used in the Atlantic world claimed that bondage benefited the enslaved by keeping them under “superior” guidance. Opposition to serfdom seemed almost cautious, with abolitionists agreeing that serfdom was not as extreme as black slavery. The debate seemed less about if peasants should be subordinated and more about how.


2)    How did these arguments transform over time, especially when used by Estonian writers? 

Over time, especially in the 19th century, Estonian commentators transformed pro-serfdom arguments to fight for sovereignty. Baltic-Germans had claimed serfdom was “necessary discipline,” and beneficial but Estonian writers reversed the claims as evidence of German oppression and exploitation. They argued that instead of proving peasant inferiority, the resilience of Estonians under serfdom was proof of their strength and capacity for nationhood. Arguments that had been used to justifiy inequality were reframed as a call for cultural revival and political rights. The narrative of peasant inferiority became less accepted, and the peasants’ perspective began to come to the forefront.


3)    In your country/community/etc who gets to tell the story of historical (in)equality? Has it been contested like in the case of Estonia? Are there historical narratives in your culture that justify inequality the way Baltic-German elites did? Are those narratives challenged today? If so, how? 

In the U.S., narratives of racial inequality have been debated since the nation’s founding. Federalists and Jeffersonian Republicans both spoke of liberty while tolerating or defending slavery, setting a contradictory foundation. Thomas Jefferson himself articulated ideals of equality in the Declaration of Independence but simultaneously rationalized Black inferiority and maintained his own enslaved labor force — echoing the Baltic-German claims that hierarchy was “natural.” The earliest abolitionists, however, challenged this from the late 18th century onward, insisting on universal freedom and exposing the hypocrisy at the heart of the republic. Abraham Lincoln later became the central figure in reframing slavery as incompatible with American democracy, though even he initially advocated gradual emancipation rather than immediate equality.

At the cultural level, figures like George Washington Carver disrupted dominant narratives by demonstrating the intellectual and creative achievements of African Americans in the face of systemic exclusion. His work in agricultural science offered a counter-story to claims of Black inferiority and provided a model of resilience and progress. Yet despite these challenges, for much of U.S. history the “official” story was told by politicians, historians, and textbooks that downplayed slavery, Jim Crow, and indigenous dispossession — much like Baltic-German elites once justified serfdom as paternalism. Today, these narratives are actively contested in battles over curricula, monuments, and public memory.


4)    (Optional) Is there anything you would prefer to be done differently in regards to the forum post tasks? 

Everything seems ok, now that I have begun to understand the system. I was a little slow to comprehend how it was going to work.

title: Wankel_Text-Discussion_War-of-Independence-to-World-War-II_Kalling_Tammiksaar
body:
1) Both the temperance movement (and the ideas behind it) as well as Darwin’s ideas were received and interpreted differently by Baltic-Germans and Estonians. Why? How did ethnicity, language, culture, class, politics and (historical) context affect this? / And what do these differences reveal about how ethnicity, cultural identity, class and (historical) context affect our perception and reception of ideas? 

The temperance movement in Estonia was shaped by class and ethnicity, and often framed as morality. For Estonians, anti-alcohol societies were used in the mission for national emancipation. Sobriety was tied to discipline, self-improvement, and the rejection of German landlords’ tavern privileges, as well as evidence of Estonian superiority. Initially, Baltic-Germans often dismissed or ignored temperance (since tavern rights were part of their economic control) before later changing in response to a shifting political climate. Thus, what was framed as a moral or health issue also became political and national.

Darwinism was received along the similar ethnic and class lines. For Baltic-Germans, it raised anxieties about both Russification from above and emancipation from below, and some scholars leaned on racialized readings of evolution to defend their own elite status. 



2) Based on the articles, how did temperance and evolutionary “fitness” become symbols of progress or cultural superiority?

Temperance became a marker of cultural maturity: Estonians used sobriety as proof of their worthiness for autonomy. For Baltic-Germans indifference to temperance reinforced a stereotype of decadence. Evolutionary fitness was often used to argue for superiority. Estonians stressed collective improvement through discipline and education. Baltic-Germans stressed racial purity. In both cases, “progress” was not neutral but was framed in ways that reinforced each group’s claim to superiority.

Darwinism and the temperance movement were joined in many ways in the 1890s. Temperance began as a moral and economic movement but soon adopted arguments from science including degeneration theory and genetics. For Estonians, staying sober was connected to survival, as a small nation with low birth rates and stronger neighbors. Darwin’s ideas of fitness and extinction gave outlets to express this fear. Alcohol was seen as weakening the people and discipline showed strength. Over time, temperance and evolutionary thinking blended into a nationalist program of self-preservation. Baltic-Germans often used Darwin to argue for their racial superiority, but Estonians flipped the narrative and used the same language to argue for their own survival and improvement.




3) Are there examples of social movements, scientific theories, moral campaigns etc. in the history of your country/community that were received differently by different groups? Were these situations similar to how the articles presented the situation in Estonia?

Yes. In the United States, Puritan moral campaigns against drinking and immorality in the 19th century resonated more with middle-class Anglo-Protestants than with immigrant communities who viewed them as attacks on their culture. Darwinism was fiercely contested with educated elites embracing it as scientific modernity, while many religious communities resisted it as threatening Biblical authority. The Scopes Trial (1925) is parallel to Estonian debates where the same scientific theory was framed either as progress or as moral corruption, depending on culture and class identity. The way Estonians deployed temperance and Baltic-Germans racialized Darwin is similar to how different groups of Americans used Puritanism and creationism to define moral boundaries and social hierarchy.
